What Is a Confidence Interval?
A confidence interval (CI) is a range of plausible values for the population mean \(\mu\), built around our sample mean

○ A 95% CI: if we repeated the study many times, 95% of the intervals built this way would contain \(\mu\)


○ It uses the same \(z\) cutoffs you already know

title: Confidence Intervals & Effect Size
text:
The CI Formula
\[\text{CI} = \bar{x} \pm z^{*} \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]

○ \(\bar{x}\): the sample mean, the center of the interval


○ \(z^{*}\): the cutoff for our confidence level (1.96 for 95%)


○ \(s / \sqrt{n}\): the standard error


Lower bound \(= \bar{x} - z^{*} \times SE\) Upper bound \(= \bar{x} + z^{*} \times SE\)

ⓘ Why the minus? The lower cutoff is \(-1.96\), so \(\bar{x} + (-1.96) \times SE\) is the same as \(\bar{x} - 1.96 \times SE\)

title: Confidence Intervals & Effect Size
text:
CIs and NHST
A 95% CI and a two-tailed test with \(\alpha\) = .05 always agree:

○ The CI excludes \(\mu_0\) → reject \(H_0\) (\(p\) < .05)


○ The CI includes \(\mu_0\) → fail to reject \(H_0\)


Example: someone claims the mean petal length is \(\mu_0\) = 3.3 cm
Our 95% CI is [3.48, 4.04]. Is 3.3 inside?


No → reject \(H_0\): the mean petal length differs from 3.3 cm

title: Confidence Intervals & Effect Size
text:
z- vs. t-Distribution
When we don’t know \(\sigma\) (almost always!), we estimate it with \(s\) and use the t-distribution

○ Bell-shaped and symmetric, but with thicker tails


○ Its shape depends on the degrees of freedom: \(df = n - 1\)


○ As \(df\) increases, it looks more and more like the standard normal (\(z\)) distribution


○ With \(df = \infty\), it is exactly the normal distribution, so with a large \(df\), \(t \approx z\)

title: Confidence Intervals & Effect Size
text:
The One-Sample t-Test
Same idea as the \(z\)-test, but with \(s\) in place of \(\sigma\):
\[t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s / \sqrt{n}}, \qquad df = n - 1\]
R does every step for us with t.test():
t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")

○ x: the sample data


○ mu: the population mean under \(H_0\) (default 0)


○ alternative: "two.sided" (default), "less", or "greater"

title: Confidence Intervals & Effect Size
text:
t.test() Example: Highway MPG
A researcher claims cars average 30 highway mpg. Test it with the 234 cars in mpg$hwy (we don’t know \(\sigma\)). One- or two-tailed?












Two-tailed: the claim gives no direction
\(t\)(233) = −16.85, \(p\) < .001 → reject \(H_0\)


Pull out pieces with $:
result$statistic
result$p.value
result$conf.int
The 95% CI [22.67, 24.21] excludes 30, so the CI tells the same story

title: Confidence Intervals & Effect Size
text:
One-Tailed t.test()
What if the researcher had predicted, before looking, that cars get less than 30 mpg?












○ "less" → \(H_1\): \(\mu\) < 30 (lower tail)


○ "greater" → \(H_1\): \(\mu\) > 30 (upper tail)


The one-tailed \(p\) is half the two-tailed \(p\), and the CI becomes one-sided: (−Inf, 24.08]

title: Confidence Intervals & Effect Size
text:
Statistical vs. Practical Significance

○ Statistical significance: is there any difference?


○ Practical significance: how big is the difference?

With a big enough \(n\), even a tiny difference is significant, so we also report an effect size: the size of the effect, independent of sample size
\[d = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{s}\]



\(|d|\)
Effect size




0.2
Small


0.5
Medium


0.8
Large




ⓘ Unlike \(t\), there is no \(\sqrt{n}\): we divide by the SD, not the standard error. Cohen’s d is a description, not a test

text:
Cohen’s d in R: Highway MPG











ⓘ R’s built-in Cohen’s d functions are mostly for comparing two groups, so we compute the one-sample d by hand



\(d\) = −1.10: a large effect. Cars average about 1.1 SDs below the claimed 30 mpg

○ Increasing the sample size increases the effect size: False


○ A larger difference between \(\bar{x}\) and \(\mu\) increases the effect size: True (it is the numerator)

title: Confidence Intervals & Effect Size
text:
Must-Take-Home Message

○ A CI = \(\bar{x} \pm\) cutoff × SE. Higher confidence → wider interval


○ A 95% CI that excludes \(\mu_0\) ↔︎ reject \(H_0\) in a two-tailed test at \(\alpha\) = .05


○ \(\sigma\) unknown → use \(s\) and the \(t\)-distribution (\(df = n - 1\)); qt() for cutoffs, t.test() for the whole test


○ Significance asks is there an effect?; Cohen’s \(d = (\bar{x} - \mu) / s\) asks how big? (.2 small, .5 medium, .8 large)

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing I
text:
Two Distributions, Two z-Scores


Distribution of the data

○ Score: \(x\)


○ Mean: \(\mu\), SD: \(\sigma\)


○ \(z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\) (Lab 4!)


Sampling distribution

○ Score: \(\bar{x}\)


○ Mean: \(\mu\), SE: \(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\)


○ \(z_{\bar{x}} = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}\)



The second one is our test statistic: how many standard errors is our sample mean away from the hypothesized population mean?

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing I
section: Putting It Together: How Likely Is Our Sample Mean?
text:
Putting It Together: How Likely Is Our Sample Mean?
Back to our example: \(\mu\) = 10, \(\sigma\) = 2, \(n\) = 20, \(\bar{x}\) = 12. If the population mean really is 10, how likely is a sample mean this far from it?











Three steps: SE → z → pnorm()

The area is tiny (about 4 in a million): a mean of 12 would be very unlikely if \(\mu\) were 10


Same answer without making the z first, using the sampling distribution directly:
pnorm(12, mean = 10, sd = 2 / sqrt(20), lower.tail = F)


Now try pop_sd <- 8: how does the probability change?

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing I
text:
Must-Take-Home Message
\[z_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}\]

○ The z-statistic counts how many standard errors \(\bar{x}\) is from \(\mu\)


○ pnorm() turns a z into a probability (area under the curve); use lower.tail = F or -abs(z) for the upper tail


○ qnorm() turns a probability into a z: ±1.96 (two-tailed), ±1.65 (one-tailed)


○ Two-tailed p = 2 × one-tailed p

text:
Where Does R Look for Files? The Working Directory

When you write read.csv("student_data.csv"), R reads it as: “look for student_data.csv inside the current working directory”


Rule for beginners

Your R Markdown file and all required data files should be placed in the same assignment folder before you begin working.

Lab_03/
├── Lab_03.Rmd
└── student_data.csv
Then loading the data only needs the file name:

student_data <- read.csv("student_data.csv")


Check before you load data

getwd()        # which folder is R looking in?
list.files()   # which files can R see there?

If the setup is correct you should see something like:
[1] "/Users/yourname/Documents/Lab_03"
[1] "Lab_03.Rmd"  "student_data.csv"

○ Tip: when you knit an .Rmd, the working directory is the folder the .Rmd is saved in

title: Measures of Variability
text:
The Common Mistake



Files downloaded to different places
Downloads/
└── Lab_03.Rmd

Desktop/
└── student_data.csv
The working directory is Downloads, so this fails:

read.csv("student_data.csv")

Error in file(file, "rt") : cannot open the connection
In addition: Warning message:
  cannot open file 'student_data.csv': No such file or directory

What the error means
R looked in the working directory but did not find a file with that exact name.
The fix

○ Move both files into the same folder (e.g., Lab_03/)


○ Open the .Rmd from that folder


○ Re-run getwd() and list.files() to confirm


Fix the folder, not the code: don’t keep rewriting the path in read.csv().
Also check the exact file name: Student_Data.csv ≠ student_data.csv

Measures of Variability in R
Variance: Average of the squared distances of each value from the mean \(s^2 = \dfrac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}\)
Standard deviation: Square root of the variance; the typical distance of a value from the mean, in the original units
Quantile: A cut point that splits sorted data into equal-sized groups (e.g., 25% of values fall below the 1st quartile, 75% below the 3rd)
IQR: 3rd quartile minus 1st quartile; the range of the middle 50% of the data

title: Sampling Distributions & the Central Limit Theorem
text:
Population Parameters
Population parameters are…

○ Assumed to be constant (fixed)


○ Unknown and unknowable


○ Estimated using statistics


ⓘ μ (mu; mean) and σ (sigma; standard deviation) are parameters of the normal distribution; different distributions have different parameters


Statistics is the science of testing hypotheses about values of these (and other) parameters

○ Point estimation


○ Interval estimation

title: Sampling Distributions & the Central Limit Theorem
text:
Two Types of Estimation


Point estimation
A single value (point) estimate of the parameter’s true value

○ e.g., \(\hat{\mu} = 52\)


○ \(\hat{\mu}\) and \(M\) both refer to the sample estimate of the mean


Interval estimation
A range of values that may contain the population parameter

○ e.g., \(\hat{\mu} = (100, 150)\)


○ Usually reported with a confidence level (e.g., 95%) to indicate the method’s reliability



If we drew 100 random samples and computed a 95% confidence interval (CI) for each one, we would expect about 95 of those 100 CIs to include the true population mean

title: Sampling Distributions & the Central Limit Theorem
text:
Let’s Get a Sample


A sample consists of multiple observations drawn from the population
\[X_1, X_2, X_3, \dots, X_{n}\]
We summarize the sample with its sample mean
\[\bar{X} = \frac{\sum x}{n}\]

title: Sampling Distributions & the Central Limit Theorem
text:
Sampling Distribution


Multiple means from multiple samples
\[\bar{X}_1, \bar{X}_2, \bar{X}_3, \dots\]
The distribution of those means is the sampling distribution
. . .
…and it is (approximately) a normal distribution!

○ Unimodal, symmetrical


○ Mean = median = mode


○ 68% / 95% / 99.7% within 1 / 2 / 3 SDs

What the Sampling Distribution Tells Us
It allows us to…

○ specify a range of scores the population mean is expected to fall within


○ determine how accurate our sample mean is in estimating the true population mean


○ determine how likely an observed statistic (e.g., a sample mean) is, assuming some hypothesized parameter holds in the population

title: Sampling Distributions & the Central Limit Theorem
text:
Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
Definition: if you take sufficiently large random samples from the population, then the distribution of the sample means will be approximately normally distributed

ⓘ It doesn’t have to be a mean for the CLT to hold. It can also be a sum (a sum is part of calculating the mean!)


Two things I want to point out:

Repeatedly sampling from a non-normal population still gives you a normal sampling distribution
The variance of the sampling distribution is smaller than the original variance

2) Sampling Variance < Original Variance
The variance of the sampling distribution of the mean is always smaller than the original population variance

○ Less variability in the sample means than in the population


○ As the sample size increases, the sampling distribution becomes narrower


Because the original variance is divided by \(n\), the sample size:

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing II
text:
Steps 4–5: Sample (\(n - 1\)) or Population (\(N\))?


Sample (most of our data!)
Step 4. Variance: divide SS by \(n - 1\)
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1} = \frac{8}{3 - 1} = 4\]
Step 5. SD: take the square root
\[s = \sqrt{4} = 2\]

Population (every member measured)
Step 4. Variance: divide SS by \(N\)
\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x - \mu)^2}{N} = \frac{8}{3} \approx 2.667\]
Step 5. SD: take the square root
\[\sigma = \sqrt{2.667} \approx 1.633\]


ⓘ Common midterm mistake: dividing a sample’s SS by \(n\). For a sample, divide by \(n - 1\). R’s var() and sd() already do this

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing II
text:
The Logic of Hypothesis Testing


1. State the hypotheses

○ \(H_0\): no effect (e.g., \(\mu\) = 100)


○ \(H_1\): an effect (e.g., \(\mu \neq\) 100)

2. Set \(\alpha\) = .05 and find the critical value
3. Compute \(z\) and its p-value, assuming \(H_0\) is true
4. Make a decision









Decision




\(p \le \alpha\) or \(|z| \ge |z_{crit}|\)
Reject \(H_0\) (significant)


\(p > \alpha\) or \(|z| < |z_{crit}|\)
Fail to reject \(H_0\) (not significant)



ⓘ Never say we “accept” \(H_0\) or that \(H_0\) is true

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing II
text:
Example: Weight of
Normal cats: \(\mu\) = 100 g, \(\sigma\) = 40. A sample of \(n\) = 16 cats with prenatal alcohol exposure has \(\bar{x}\) = 70. Does alcohol affect birth weight?












\(z\) = −3 is far in the rejection region
\(p\) < .05 → reject \(H_0\)
Prenatal alcohol exposure has a statistically significant effect on cats’ birth weight


ⓘ Lecture reports the one-tail area, pnorm(-3) = .00135; two-tailed p = .0027. Same decision

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing II
text:
What Does the p-Value Mean?
The p-value is the probability of getting a test statistic equal to or more extreme than the one we observed, assuming \(H_0\) is true

Cats: assuming \(\mu\) = 100 is true, the probability of a sample mean (\(n\) = 16) at least as far from 100 as 70 is











○ The smaller the p-value, the stronger the evidence against \(H_0\)


○ It is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing II
text:
Directional vs. Non-Directional Hypotheses


Non-directional → two-tailed test
“There is a difference…”

○ \(H_1\): \(\mu \neq \mu_0\)


○ \(\alpha\)/2 = .025 in each tail


○ \(z_{crit}\) = ±1.96


Directional → one-tailed test
“…increases / decreases / better than…”

○ \(H_1\): \(\mu > \mu_0\) (upper) or \(\mu < \mu_0\) (lower)


○ all of \(\alpha\) = .05 in one tail


○ \(z_{crit}\) = +1.65 or −1.65

Your Turn: The “Evil” Professor
Your professor believes extra homework changes final exam scores. Population: \(\mu\) = 70, \(\sigma\) = 15. A sample of \(n\) = 25 students who got 50 extra HW questions a week scored \(\bar{x}\) = 75.









Check: \(z = \dfrac{75 - 70}{15 / \sqrt{25}} = \dfrac{5}{3}\) = 1.67, which is less than 1.96 → retain \(H_0\)

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing II
text:
The “Evil” Professor, Revisited
Now your professor believes extra homework increases final exam scores (same data: \(\mu\) = 70, \(\sigma\) = 15, \(n\) = 25, \(\bar{x}\) = 75)











Same data, same \(z\) = 1.67…


○ Two-tailed: 1.67 < 1.96 → retain \(H_0\)


○ Upper-tailed: 1.67 > 1.65 → reject \(H_0\)



This is why the direction must be decided before looking at the data!

Type I and Type II Errors









\(H_0\) true (no effect)
\(H_0\) false (effect exists)




Reject \(H_0\)

Correct: power (\(1 - \beta\))


Fail to reject \(H_0\)
Correct

○ \(\alpha\) = probability of a Type I error; we choose it (.05)

○ Power = \(1 - \beta\) = probability of detecting a real effect

Simulating Power
Now suppose extra homework really raises the mean to 75. We still test \(H_0\): \(\mu\) = 70. How often do we catch the effect?











Every rejection here is correct, so the proportion is the power

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing II
text:
What Affects Power?











Power goes up with

○ a larger difference from \(\mu_0\)


○ less variability (\(\sigma\))


○ a larger \(n\)


○ a larger \(\alpha\)


Learning check: testing \(H_0\): \(\mu\) = 80, which is most likely to reject? (A) \(\sigma\) = 5, \(n\) = 25 (B) \(\sigma\) = 5, \(n\) = 50 (C) \(\sigma\) = 10, \(n\) = 25 (D) \(\sigma\) = 10, \(n\) = 50

Your Turn: The Popcorn Problem
A theater owner knows a bag should hold \(\mu\) = 8 cups, \(\sigma\) = 0.50. The newest employee’s \(n\) = 25 bags average \(\bar{x}\) = 7.75 cups. Is the employee filling bags incorrectly (\(\alpha\) = .05)?

title: Null Hypothesis Significance Testing II
text:
Must-Take-Home Message

○ The p-value: the probability of a result this extreme or more, assuming \(H_0\) is true


○ Directional hypothesis → one-tailed test (±1.65); non-directional → two-tailed (±1.96); decide before collecting data


○ Type I error = rejecting a true \(H_0\) (rate = \(\alpha\)); Type II error = missing a real effect (rate = \(\beta\))


○ Power = \(1 - \beta\); it goes up with a bigger difference, smaller \(\sigma\), bigger \(n\), bigger \(\alpha\)
